en: 7. The Pairs on Latent Dispositions (Anusayayamaka) 7.2 The Major Section (Mahāvāra) 7.2.2 The Section on Those Possessing Latent Dispositions (Sānusayavāra)
7.2.2.1. Positive Person (Anulomapuggala) Is one who possesses the underlying tendency to sensual lust also possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.
Or again, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to aversion also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust? Yes.
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency to sensual lust also possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Or, conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to conceit also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

A non-returner possesses the underlying tendency to conceit, but does not possess the underlying tendency to sensual lust. Three types of persons possess both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward sensual lust also possessed of the underlying tendency toward views...

[and so on] ...also possessed of the underlying tendency toward doubt? Two types of persons possess the underlying tendency toward sensual lust, but they do not possess the underlying tendency toward doubt. An ordinary worldling (puthujjana) possesses both the underlying tendency toward sensual lust and the underlying tendency toward doubt.
Or, conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency toward doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency toward sensual lust? Yes, he is.

Is one who possesses the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya)… [and so on] …the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to ignorance also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

A non-returner (anāgāmī) possesses the underlying tendency to ignorance, but does not possess the underlying tendency to sensual lust. Three types of persons possess both the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya)? Yes.
Or, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to conceit also possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion?

A non-returner (anāgāmī) possesses the underlying tendency to conceit, but does not possess the underlying tendency to aversion. Three types of persons possess both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) ... pe ... the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?

Two types of persons are possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion, but not possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt. An ordinary worldling (puthujjana) is possessed of both the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to doubt.
Or, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.

Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward aversion also possessed of the underlying tendency toward attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency toward ignorance (*avijjā*)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency toward ignorance also possessed of the underlying tendency toward aversion?

A non-returner (*anāgāmī*) possesses the underlying tendency toward ignorance, but does not possess the underlying tendency toward aversion. Three types of persons possess both the underlying tendency toward ignorance and the underlying tendency toward aversion.
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency of views (diṭṭhānusaya) ... [and] the underlying tendency of doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?

Three types of persons possess the underlying tendency of conceit, but they do not possess the underlying tendency of doubt. The worldling (puthujjana) possesses both the underlying tendency of conceit and the underlying tendency of doubt.
Or, is one who possesses the underlying tendency of doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency of conceit? Yes.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya)… [and] the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Yes.
Or, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance also possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)? Yes.
Or, whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya), is that person possessed of the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya)? Yes, they are. ... [as before] ...

Whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt, is that person possessed of the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya) ... [as before] ... and the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Yes, they are.
Or, whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, is that person possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt?

Three types of persons possess the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), but do not possess the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*). An ordinary worldling (*puthujjana*) possesses both the underlying tendency of ignorance and the underlying tendency of doubt.
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) necessarily possessed of the underlying tendency of ignorance? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency of ignorance necessarily possessed of the underlying tendency of attachment to existence? Yes. (Based on a single root.)
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Or, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?

A non-returner is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit, but is not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion. Three types of persons are possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit and are also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward sensual lust and the underlying tendency toward aversion also possessed of the underlying tendency toward views ... pe ... and the underlying tendency toward doubt?
Two types of persons possess the underlying tendency toward sensual lust and the underlying tendency toward aversion, but they do not possess the underlying tendency toward doubt.
A worldling (puthujjana), however, possesses the underlying tendency toward sensual lust, the underlying tendency toward aversion, and also possesses the underlying tendency toward doubt.
Or, whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt is also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.

Whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion is also possessed of the underlying tendency to existence … pe … and the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or, whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance is also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?

The non-returner (anāgāmī) is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya), but he is not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) nor the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya).

Three types of persons are possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance and are also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion. (End of the section based on pairs.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) …pe… the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?
Two types of persons are possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit,

but they are not possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt. The worldling is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and also the underlying tendency to doubt.
Alternatively, is one who possesses the underlying tendency of doubt also possessed of the underlying tendencies of sensual lust, aversion, and conceit? Yes.
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendencies of sensual lust, aversion, and conceit also possessed of the underlying tendencies of existence-lust ... pe ... and ignorance? Yes.
Alternatively, is one who possesses the underlying tendency of ignorance also possessed of the underlying tendencies of sensual lust, aversion, and conceit?

The non-returner (anāgāmī) is still possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) and the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya), but he is not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya).
Three types of persons are possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, and they are also possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit.
(End of the section based on triplets.)

Is one who possesses the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, also possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views? Yes. ... [End of] the Section Based on Fourfold Roots.

Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward sensual lust, ill will, conceit, views, and doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency toward existence, and so forth, up to the underlying tendency toward ignorance? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency toward ignorance also possessed of the underlying tendencies toward sensual lust, ill will, conceit, views, and doubt?

The non-returner (anāgāmī) is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) and the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya), but he is not possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya),
aversion (paṭighānusaya), views (diṭṭhānusaya), and doubt (vicikicchānusaya). Two types of persons are possessed of the underlying tendencies to ignorance,
sensual lust, aversion, and conceit, but they are not possessed of the underlying tendency to views.
And [the worldling] is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt.
The worldling is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, and he is possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, and doubt. (The pentad-based section.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, also possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or again, whoever is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya), is he also possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (kāmarāga), resentment (paṭigha), conceit (māna), views (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), and lust for existence (bhavarāga)?

A non-returner (anāgāmī) is possessed of the underlying tendencies to ignorance, conceit, and lust for existence, but he is not possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, resentment, views, and doubt. [This applies to] two types of persons.

They possess the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence;
yet they do not possess the underlying tendency to views nor the underlying tendency to doubt.
The worldling possesses the underlying tendency to ignorance, as well as the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and views.
And one who possesses the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to lust for existence is "with underlying tendencies. (The Sixfold Rooted Section. 7.2.2.2.
Positive Plane:
Wherever one is with the underlying tendency to lust for sense-pleasures, is one there with the underlying tendency to aversion? No.
Or, conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya)? No.
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency to sensual lust also possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya)? Yes.
Or, conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency to conceit also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

In the fine-material element (*rūpadhātu*) and the immaterial element (*arūpadhātu*), one is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) there, but not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) there. In the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*), in two types of feeling, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit there and also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust there.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust there also possessed of the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) there? Yes.
Or, conversely, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt there also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust there?
In the unpleasant feeling, in the form element, and in the formless element, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt with respect to those,
but not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to them. In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu),
one is possessed of both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to them.
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya)? No.
Or rather, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust? No.
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Yes.
Or again, is one who is latent with the underlying tendency of ignorance also latent with the underlying tendency of sensual lust?

In the case of painful feeling, in the fine-material element, and in the immaterial element, one is latent with the underlying tendency of ignorance there, but not latent with the underlying tendency of sensual lust.
In the sense-sphere element, in the two types of feeling, one is latent with both the underlying tendency of ignorance and the underlying tendency of sensual lust.
One who possesses the underlying tendency to sensual lust also possesses the underlying tendency [to ignorance].
Is it the case that wherever one possesses the underlying tendency to aversion, one also possesses the underlying tendency to conceit? No.
Or rather, is it the case that wherever one possesses the underlying tendency to conceit, one also possesses the underlying tendency to aversion? No.

Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward aversion (paṭigha) also possessed of the underlying tendency toward views (diṭṭhi), and so on, up to the underlying tendency toward doubt (vicikicchā)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency toward doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency toward aversion?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) and formless-sphere realm (arūpadhātu), one is possessed of the underlying tendency toward doubt, but not necessarily of the underlying tendency toward aversion.

And yet, one is not thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*). Regarding painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*), one is thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) and also possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion.
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)? No.

Or, from whatever [state] one is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), is one therefrom possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)? No.
From whatever [state] one is possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion, is one therefrom possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*)? Yes.
Or, from whatever [state] one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, is one therefrom possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion?
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless-sphere realm (arūpadhātu),

one is latent with the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya), but not latent with the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya). In painful feeling, one is latent both with the underlying tendency to ignorance and with the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward conceit (māna) also possessed of the underlying tendency toward views (diṭṭhi) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency toward doubt (vicikicchā)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency toward doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency toward conceit?
In the case of painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā), one is possessed of the underlying tendency toward doubt there, but not possessed of the underlying tendency toward conceit.
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere (rūpadhātu) and formless-sphere (arūpadhātu),

one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt is also possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit. Is it the case that wherever one is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit, one is also possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāga)?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), one is latent with respect to that underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya), but not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya). In the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), one is latent both with respect to the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to lust for existence.
Is it the case that wherever one is latent with respect to the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one is also latent with respect to the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is it the case that wherever one is latent with respect to the underlying tendency to conceit, one is also latent with respect to the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is subject to the underlying tendency of ignorance also subject to the underlying tendency of conceit?
In the case of painful feeling, one is subject to the underlying tendency of ignorance there, but not subject to the underlying tendency of conceit.

In the two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), and in the form-sphere realm (*rūpadhātu*) and formless-sphere realm (*arūpadhātu*), one is subject both to the underlying tendency of ignorance and [to the underlying tendency of conceit].

And one who possesses the underlying tendency of conceit also possesses [other] underlying tendencies. Is one who possesses the underlying tendency of views also possessed of the underlying tendency of doubt? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who possesses the underlying tendency of doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency of views? Yes … [and so on].
Is one who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward doubt also possessed of the underlying tendency toward attachment to existence (bhavarāga)?
One who possesses the underlying tendency toward doubt in the three feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) is not, however, possessed of the underlying tendency toward attachment to existence.

But one who possesses the underlying tendency toward doubt in the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu) is also possessed of the underlying tendency toward attachment to existence.
Or, where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence, is one there possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence, is one there possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or, where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, is one there possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is latent with the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya) but not latent with the underlying tendency of lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya).
In the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial sphere (arūpadhātu), one is latent both with the underlying tendency of ignorance and the underlying tendency of lust for existence.
(End of the section based on a single root.)
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also, therefore, possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit? No.
Or rather, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit also, therefore, possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit, but not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

And [is one] with underlying tendency toward aversion? In two feelings within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one has underlying tendencies toward the underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*) and the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), but one does not have an underlying tendency toward aversion there.

Is one who has underlying tendencies toward both the underlying tendency of sensual lust and the underlying tendency of aversion also with underlying tendencies toward the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? No.
Or again, is one who is latent with the underlying tendency of doubt also latent with the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is latent with the underlying tendency of doubt, but not latent with the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and aversion.
In the sense-sphere element, in two types of feeling, one is latent with the underlying tendency of doubt...
One who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust is not, therefore, possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion.
One who is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion regarding painful feeling is not, therefore, possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, therefore, possessed of the underlying tendency to existence? No.

Or, where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), is one there also possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*)? No.

Where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure and the underlying tendency to aversion, is one there also possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*)? There is none.
Or, where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, is one there also possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for sensual pleasure and the underlying tendency to aversion?

In the form realm and the formless realm, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) with respect to those [realms], but one is not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) with respect to them.

In the two feelings of the sense realm (kāmadhātu), one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance and the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to them, but one is not possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion with respect to them. In the feeling of pain (dukkhā vedanā)...

Then, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), but one is not thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*). (The section based on pairs.

Wherever one is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), is one there possessed of the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)? No.

Or conversely, wherever one is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt, is one there possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is latent with respect to that [state] through the underlying tendency of doubt and the underlying tendency of conceit,
but not through the underlying tendency of sensual lust and the underlying tendency of aversion. In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element,
one is latent with respect to that [state] through the underlying tendency of doubt, the underlying tendency of sensual lust, and the underlying tendency of conceit, but not through that...

One is possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya). In regard to painful feeling, one is possessed of both the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) and the underlying tendency to aversion, but not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya).
Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit necessarily possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya)? No.

Or, from whatever state one is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence, is one then possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit? One is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit.
From whatever state one is possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit, is one then possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance? There is none.
Or, from whatever state one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, is one then possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit?

In the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), one is latent with respect to that [state] regarding the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) and the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya),
but not regarding the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya). In the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu), in two types of feeling,

one is latent with respect to that [state] regarding the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to conceit, but not regarding the underlying tendency to aversion.

One who possesses latent tendencies (*sānusaya*): with respect to painful feeling, one possesses latent tendencies there through the latent tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) and the latent tendency of resistance (*paṭighānusaya*), but one does not possess latent tendencies there through the latent tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the latent tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*). (End of the section based on the triad.

Is one who possesses latent tendencies through the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of resistance, the latent tendency of conceit, and the latent tendency of views, also necessarily possessed of the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) therein? No.
Or, conversely, where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt, is one there also possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and views?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is possessed of the underlying tendencies to doubt, conceit, and views, but not possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion. In the sense-sphere element...
In two types of feeling, one is possessed of the underlying tendency (anusaya) toward doubt, sensual lust, conceit, and views;
yet one is not possessed of the underlying tendency toward aversion. In painful feeling, one is possessed of the underlying tendencies toward doubt, aversion, and views;
yet one is not possessed of the underlying tendency toward sensual lust.

One who is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) is also possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (kāmarāga), aversion (paṭigha), views (diṭṭhi), and existence (bhavarāga). Is it the case that wherever one is possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and views, one is thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to existence? No.

Or conversely, is it the case that wherever one is possessed of the underlying tendency to existence, one is thereby possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and views? No.
One who possesses the underlying tendency (anusaya) of conceit and the underlying tendency of views—does that person, from that same state, possess the underlying tendency of ignorance? No.
Or conversely, one who possesses the underlying tendency of ignorance—does that person, from that same state, possess the underlying tendencies of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and views? No.
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views;
however, one is not possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion therein.

In the sense-sphere element, within two types of feeling, one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views therein.
And one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, but not possessed of the underlying tendency to aversion from that [feeling].

In regard to painful feeling, one is possessed of the underlying tendencies to ignorance, aversion, and views from that [feeling], but not possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and conceit from that [feeling]. (End of the section based on four roots.)

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, also possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence? No.

Or conversely, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to lust for existence also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?
One is possessed of the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt.

Is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt, thereby also possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance? No.

Or conversely, is one who is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance thereby also possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt?

[Yes,] except in the fine-material element and the immaterial element, where one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views.
One is still possessed of the underlying tendency to doubt, yet not thereby possessed of the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and ill will.
In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is possessed of the underlying tendencies to ignorance,
sensual lust, conceit, views, and doubt, yet not thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to ill will.

In regard to unpleasant feeling, one is still possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt;
yet one is not thereby possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to conceit. (End of the Section Based on Five.

Is it the case that wherever one is possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, one is there also possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance? No, there is none.

Or, conversely, since one is possessed of the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*), is one then possessed of the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*), the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*), and the underlying tendency to lust for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*)?

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

Two types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt, but not free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust. Two types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt and also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to existence (bhavarāgānusaya)… [and] the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?

The non-returner (anāgāmī) is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, but not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance. The arahant is free from both the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Or, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya)?

An Anāgāmī is free from the underlying tendency to aversion, but not free from the underlying tendency to conceit. An Arahant is free from both the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to conceit.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit also free from the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) … pe … and free from the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to aversion?

Two types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt but not free from the underlying tendency to aversion. Two types of persons are free from both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to existence-attachment (bhavarāgānusaya) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?

The non-returner (anāgāmī) is free from the underlying tendency to aversion, but not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance. The Arhat (arahā) is free from both the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) ... [and] the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to conceit?

Three types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt, but not free from the underlying tendency to conceit. The Arahat is free from both the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to conceit.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya)… [and so on] …free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)? Yes.
Or again, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya)? Yes. ... [as before] ...

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) ... up to ... the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?

Three types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt, but they are not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance. An Arhat is both free from the underlying tendency to doubt and free from the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Or, whoever is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance, is that person also free from the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Whoever is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence, is that person also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or, whoever is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance, is that person also free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes. (Based on a single root.)
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also free from the underlying tendency to conceit?

An Anāgāmī is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, but not free from the underlying tendency to conceit. An Arahant is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also free from the underlying tendency to views … pe … the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion?
Two types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt, but they are not free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

And [they] are free from underlying tendencies. Two types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt and are also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also free from the underlying tendency to existence, ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to ignorance?

The non-returner is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, but he is not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance. The arahant is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, and he is also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance.

Or, whoever is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance, is that person also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes. (End of the Section Based on Pairs.

Whoever is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, is that person also free from the underlying tendency to views … [and so on] … the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.

Or, whoever is free from the underlying tendency to doubt, is that person also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit?
Two types of persons are free from the underlying tendency to doubt, yet they are not free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit.

The non-returner is free from the underlying tendencies to doubt, sensual lust, and aversion, yet he is not free from the underlying tendency to conceit. The arahant [is free from the underlying tendency to doubt]...
And one who is free from underlying tendencies is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit also free from the underlying tendency to existence, ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes. (The Section Based on the Triad.)

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to wrong view, also free from the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to wrong view?
There are two types of persons who are free from the underlying tendency to doubt and the underlying tendency to wrong view, yet they are not free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
And [the Non-returner] is free from underlying tendencies toward resentment and underlying tendency toward conceit.

The Non-returner is free from underlying tendencies toward doubt, underlying tendency toward sensual lust, underlying tendency toward resentment, and underlying tendency toward views, but he is not free from underlying tendency toward conceit.

The Arhat is free from underlying tendencies toward doubt, and [is also free] from underlying tendency toward sensual lust, underlying tendency toward resentment, and underlying tendency toward conceit.
...and is free from the underlying tendency to views ... [as before] ... (The Section Based on Four).

Is one who is free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, and doubt also free from the underlying tendency to existence ... [as before] ... and the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, and doubt? Yes. (The Section Based on Five).

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes. (The Sixfold Rooted Section.)
7.2.2.5. Negative Order (Paṭiloma-okāsa) Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya)?
In regard to painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā), one is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, but not free from the underlying tendency to aversion.

In the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), and the unconditioned (apariyāpanna), one is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and also free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya).
Or, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust?
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion, but not [necessarily] free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
One who is free from the underlying tendency toward aversion in the fine-material element, the immaterial element, and the unconditioned (apariyāpanna),
is also free from the underlying tendency toward sensual lust in those realms.
Is it the case that wherever one is free from the underlying tendency toward sensual lust, one is also free from the underlying tendency toward conceit?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust, yet one is not, therefore, non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to conceit.

In painful feeling and in the unperturbed (apariyāpanna), one is both non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust and non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to conceit. Or, conversely:
Is one who is non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to conceit also non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust? Yes.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?

In regard to painful feeling, the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust there, but not free from the underlying tendency to doubt.
In the supramundane (apariyāpanna), one is free from both the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to doubt.
One who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt is also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust.
Or rather, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust also free from the underlying tendency to existence?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust, yet one is not thereby not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to lust for existence.

In painful feeling and in the unperturbed (unincluded), one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust and is also not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to lust for existence.
Or, conversely, is one who is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to lust for existence also not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya), yet one is not non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure (kāmarāgānusaya).

In painful feeling and in the unconditioned (apariyāpanna), one is both non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to existence and non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure.

Is it the case that wherever one is non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure, one is also non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?
In regard to painful feeling, the fine-material element, and the immaterial element, one is not latent with the underlying tendency to sensual lust,

yet one is not non-latent with the underlying tendency to ignorance. In regard to what is not included [in the mundane], one is neither latent with the underlying tendency to sensual lust nor latent with the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Or conversely: Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya)? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya)?

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), and in the form-sphere and formless-sphere realms (rūpadhātu and arūpadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion, but [not necessarily from conceit].

And yet, one is not free from the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*) because of that [state]. In the states not included within the mundane realms (*apariyāpanna*), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) and also free from the underlying tendency to conceit.
Or rather, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit necessarily free from the underlying tendency to aversion?

With respect to painful feeling, one is not latent with the underlying tendency to conceit (*mānānusaya*), yet one is not non-latent with the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*). In the states not included [in the realms] (*apariyāpanna*), one is both non-latent with the underlying tendency to conceit and non-latent with the underlying tendency to aversion.

Is one who is non-latent with the underlying tendency to aversion also non-latent with the underlying tendency to views (*diṭṭhānusaya*) … pe … and the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*)?

In two types of feeling within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), and in the fine-material and immaterial realms (*rūpadhātu* and *arūpadhātu*), one is non-latent with the underlying tendency to aversion.

And yet, one is not free from the underlying tendency to doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*) because of that [state]. In the states not included [in the mundane] (*apariyāpanna*), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) and free from the underlying tendency to doubt.
Or rather, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes, he is.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya)?

In the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion, but not free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) and in the state that is not included [in the realms] (apariyāpanna), one is free from both the underlying tendency to aversion and the underlying tendency to attachment to existence.

And one who is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) [is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion]. Or, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion also free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence?
One is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence with respect to painful feeling, but one is not thereby free from the underlying tendency to aversion.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu) and in the unconditioned (apariyāpanna), one is free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya) and free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya).
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion in those [states] also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere, and in the form-sphere (rūpadhātu) and formless-sphere (arūpadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion.

And yet, one is not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) because of that [state]. In the states not included [in the mundane] (*apariyāpanna*), one is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*) and free from the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Or rather, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes, he is.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya) ... pe ... and the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?

In the case of painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā), one is free from the underlying tendency to conceit there, but not free from the underlying tendency to doubt there. In the unincluded (apariyāpanna) [realms], one is free from both the underlying tendency to conceit and the underlying tendency to doubt there.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya)? Yes.
Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence also free from the underlying tendency to conceit?
In the two feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence, but not from the underlying tendency to conceit.

One who is free from underlying tendencies (*niranusaya*) toward painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*) is also free from the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) and free from the underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*) in the unperturbed states (*apariyāpanna*).
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency of conceit also free from the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*)?

One is free from the underlying tendency of conceit toward painful feeling, but not free from the underlying tendency of ignorance. In the unperturbed states, one is free from both the underlying tendency of conceit and the underlying tendency of ignorance.
Or, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to views also free from the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.
Or, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to views? Yes … [and so on] …
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya)? Yes.
Or rather, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence also free from the underlying tendency to doubt?
In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence, but not free from the underlying tendency to doubt.

One who is without latent tendencies (*niranusaya*) in the supramundane states (*apariyāpanna*) is, therefore, without the latent tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) and without the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikicchānusaya*).
Is one who is without the latent tendency of doubt necessarily without the latent tendency of ignorance (*avijjānusaya*)? Yes.
Or, is one who is without the latent tendency of ignorance necessarily without the latent tendency of doubt? Yes.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?

In the three feelings of the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence, but not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance. In the states that are not included [in the realms] (apariyāpanna), one is free from both the underlying tendency to lust for existence and the underlying tendency to ignorance.
Or, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes, they are. (End of the section based on a single root.)
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion also free from the underlying tendency to conceit?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, but not free from the underlying tendency to conceit.
In the unperturbed (the supramundane), one is [free] from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion...

And one who is free from the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya) is also free from the underlying tendency of sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency of aversion (paṭighānusaya)? Or, conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency of sensual lust and the underlying tendency of aversion also free from the underlying tendency of conceit?
One is free from the underlying tendency of conceit and the underlying tendency of sensual lust with respect to painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā), but not [free] with respect to that [aversion].
One who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya) is also free from the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya) in the states not included [in the mundane] (apariyāpanna).

And one who is free from both the underlying tendency to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to aversion is also free from the underlying tendency to views (diṭṭhānusaya)…pe… and the underlying tendency to doubt (vicikicchānusaya)?
In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion,

yet one is not non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to doubt. In the unincluded (apariyāpanna), one is non-latent with respect to the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to doubt.
Or, conversely, where one is not latent with the underlying tendency to doubt, is one there also not latent with the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion? Yes.
Where one is not latent with the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, is one there also not latent with the underlying tendency to lust for existence?

In the fine-material element and the immaterial element, one is not latent with the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to aversion, [but may still be latent with the underlying tendency to lust for existence].

And yet, one is not free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) because of that [state]. In the states not included [in the mundane] (*apariyāpanna*), one is free from both the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual desire (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), and is also free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence.

But is it the case that wherever one is free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence, one is thereby also free from the underlying tendencies to attachment to sensual desire and aversion?

In regard to painful feeling, one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure (*kāmarāgānusaya*), yet one is not thereby free from the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*).

In regard to the two feelings [pleasant and neutral] within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to existence and the underlying tendency to aversion, yet one is not thereby free from the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure. In regard to the unconditioned (*apariyāpanna*)...

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya) and free from the underlying tendencies to sensual desire (kāmarāgānusaya) and aversion (paṭighānusaya) also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya)?

One is free from the underlying tendencies to sensual desire and aversion in the fine-material element (rūpadhātu) and the immaterial element (arūpadhātu), yet [in those realms] one is not necessarily free from the underlying tendency to ignorance.

And yet, one is not free from the underlying tendency to ignorance (*avijjānusaya*) because of that [state]. In the states not included [in the mundane] (*apariyāpanna*), one is free from both the underlying tendency to sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*) and the underlying tendency to aversion (*paṭighānusaya*), and is also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance.

Is it the case that wherever one is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance, one is also free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and aversion? Yes, it is so. (The Section Based on Pairs.)

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also free from the underlying tendency to views … pe … and the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to doubt also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also free from the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes.

Or, conversely, is one who is without the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya) also without the underlying tendencies to sensual desire (kāmarāgānusaya), aversion (paṭighānusaya), and conceit (mānānusaya)?
In regard to painful feeling, one is without the underlying tendencies to attachment to existence, sensual desire, and conceit, but one is not without the underlying tendency to aversion.
In regard to the two feelings within the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), one is without the underlying tendency to attachment to existence...
One is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to aversion, yet one is not free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust and conceit with respect to that [state].
In the state that is not included [within the mundane realms], one is free from the underlying tendency to existence,
and one is also free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, and conceit with respect to that.
Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit, also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.

Or conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to conceit? Yes. (End of the section based on the triad.

Is one who is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, and the underlying tendency to views, also free from the underlying tendency to doubt? Yes.

Or, where one is not latent with the underlying tendency to doubt, is one there also not latent with the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, and views? Yes. … (End of the Tetrad Rooted Section.
Where one is not latent with the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, aversion, conceit, views, and doubt, is one there also not latent with the underlying tendency to lust for existence? Yes.

Or, conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to craving for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) also free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust (kāmarāgānusaya), aversion (paṭighānusaya), conceit (mānānusaya), views (diṭṭhānusaya),
and doubt (vicikicchānusaya)? In the case of painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā), one is free from the underlying tendencies to craving for existence, sensual lust, and conceit,
but one is not free from the underlying tendencies to aversion, views, and doubt.

In the two feelings of the sense-sphere (kāmadhātu), one is not latent with respect to the underlying tendency to attachment to existence (bhavarāgānusaya) and the underlying tendency to aversion (paṭighānusaya);
yet, one is not thereby free from the underlying tendencies to attachment to sensual pleasure (kāmarāgānusaya), conceit (mānānusaya), views (diṭṭhānusaya), and doubt (vicikicchānusaya).

In the states that are not included [in the three realms] (apariyāpanna), one is free from the underlying tendency to attachment to existence, but not from the underlying tendency to attachment to sensual pleasure.
...and is one who is free from the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt ... [as before] ...
(The Section Based on Five.

Is it the case that wherever one is free from the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to lust for existence, there one is also free from the underlying tendency to ignorance? Yes.
Or, conversely, is one who is free from the underlying tendency to ignorance also free from the underlying tendencies to sensual lust, ill will, conceit, views, doubt, and lust for existence?
Yes. (The Section Based on Six.)
7.2.2.6. Negative Order:
Person and Plane Is one who is without the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to a certain [plane] also without the underlying tendency to aversion with respect to that same [plane]?

Three types of persons, in relation to painful feeling, are without the underlying tendency to sensual lust with respect to it, yet they are not without the underlying tendency to aversion with respect to it.
Those same three persons, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), the formless realm (arūpadhātu), and the unconditioned (apariyāpanna),
